extracted.intended_audience: members of Parliament, policymakers, and the informed public debating book licensing/censorship
extracted.subtask_description: A seventeenth‑century polemic arguing against prior licensing and censorship of printed books, tracing historical precedents and giving normative principles for reading, punishment, and the preservation of learning. Intended to guide legislators and public opinion on press policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition of prior licensing (no pre‑printing approval)
rubrics_metrics.description: "That no Book, pamphlet, or paper shall be henceforth Printed, unlesse the same be first approved and licenc't by such, or at least one of such as shall be thereto appointed."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text objects to any rule making prior approval a condition of printing. Examples of the Imprimatur and multiple ecclesiastical approbations are shown (several 'Imprimaturs' on title pages). The author argues this requirement is novel, imported from the Inquisition and foreign practice, impractical, and dangerous to liberty and learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post‑publication sanction for malefactor books
rubrics_metrics.description: It is of greatest concernment "to have a vigilant eye how Bookes demean themselves as well as men; and thereafter to confine, imprison, and do sharped justice on them as malefactors."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The pamphlet accepts that the state may punish books/authors after harmful effects are shown (e.g., blasphemy or libel). The distinction is drawn between retrospective punishment and preventive prior licensing: the former is legitimate, the latter is condemned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Censor chiefly for blasphemy, atheism, and libel
rubrics_metrics.description: Only two sorts of writings concerned the magistrate: "either blasphemous and Atheistickal, or Libellous."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples (burning of Protagoras, Roman actions against libels, imperial condemnations of heretical books) are used to argue that classical and early Christian authorities restricted censorship to a narrow set of offences rather than general prior control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical precedent: most states avoided prior licensing
rubrics_metrics.description: "No Nation, or well instituted State, if they valued books at all, did ever use this way of licencing..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author surveys Greek, Roman, and early Christian practice to show that broad prior licensing is neither traditional nor necessary; Plato's imagined law is treated as exceptional and not a model for polity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Books are living carriers of reason — do not destroy good books
rubrics_metrics.description: "He who destroys a good Booke, kills reason itself, kills the Image of God, as it were in the eye... a good Booke is the precious life‑blood of a master spirit, imbalm'd and treasur'd up on purpose to a life beyond life."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This moral principle underpins opposition to preventive suppression: destroying books can murder reason and harm future generations' access to truth and wisdom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensing discourages learning and halts discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Licencing "will be primely to the discouragement of all learning, and the stop of Truth, not only by the disexercising and blunting our abilities in what we know already, but by hindring and cropping the discovery that might be yet further made both in religious and civil Wisdom."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical argument: prior approval dulls intellectual exercise, prevents improvement, and chokes off future contributions and discoveries; thus it is counterproductive to the stated aims of suppressing harmful books.

rubrics_metrics.name: Readers' discretion and sufficiency of reason for mature men
rubrics_metrics.description: "Read any books whatsoever come to thy hands, for thou art sufficient both to judge aright, and to examine each matter."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton (via historical/religious examples) defends leaving reading choice to the reason and temperance of mature individuals rather than imposing legal restraints; temperance and judgement are preferred to compulsion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private voluntary destruction of one's own dangerous books permitted, not magistrate's duty
rubrics_metrics.description: The burning of the Ephesian books by converts: "It was a privat act, a voluntary act, and leaves us to a voluntary imitation: the men in remorse burnt those books which were their own; the Magistrate by this example is not appointed."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes between voluntary personal acts (permissible as conscience dictates) and state‑imposed suppression; private renunciation is acceptable but does not justify legal licensing regimes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensers cannot be assumed infallible or impartial
rubrics_metrics.description: "How shall the licencers themselves be confided in, unleese we can confer upon them, or they assume to themselves above all others in the Land, the grace of infallibility, and uncorruptednesse?"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical objection: any licensing regime depends on judgment of licensers; if they are fallible or partial, licensing will suppress truth or be abused. The pamphlet argues this makes prior licensing untrustworthy and dangerous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger of importing foreign (papal/inquisitorial) licensing models
rubrics_metrics.description: Their last invention was "to ordain that no Book, pamphlet, or paper should be Printed... unless it were approv'd and licenc't under the hands of 2 or 3 glutton Friers."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton traces the modern licensing practice to the Inquisition, the Popes, the Council of Trent and Spanish Inquisition, arguing these are tyrannous models ill-suited to English liberty and tradition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controversial theological works are dangerous mainly to the learned and need guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: "That infection which is from books of controverse in Religion, is more doubtfull and dangerous to the learned, then to the ignorant; and yet those books must be permitted untoucht by the licencer."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledges risk: learned clergy/readers are more likely to be influenced by theological controversies; however, licensing is not the right remedy — such works should be allowed but their study guided by competent teachers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Censorship is ineffective at preventing vice learned by other means
rubrics_metrics.description: "Evil manners are as perfectly learnt without books a thousand other ways which cannot be stopt, and evil doctrine not with books can propagate, except a teacher guide, which he might also doe without writing..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument that licensing will not stop moral corruption because vice is transmitted by many channels; thus prior suppression is both insufficient and misdirected as a policy tool.
